Volume 06 · Chapter 11

Exchange rates and external balances

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v06-c10

By the endConnect international accounts, exchange-rate mechanisms and policy regimes.

Capability and prerequisites

After this chapter, you can reconcile an economy's external transactions with its external balance sheet, translate an exchange-rate quote without reversing its meaning, derive covered interest parity, and explain which extra assumptions connect expectations, capital mobility and monetary regimes. You can distinguish a recorded deficit from an identified cause or a welfare judgment.

Read Trade and comparative advantage, National accounting and Money, banking and monetary transmission. We use exact gross returns and conditional expectations from earlier volumes. All numerical economies below are original synthetic cases; dates 0 and 1 are model dates, not October 2026 observations. Interest rates refer to the whole stated interval, not an unstated annualization.

1. Begin with the reporting economy and the accounting convention

An external account classifies relationships between residents and nonresidents; citizenship and currency denomination do not determine residence. A resident's foreign-currency loan from another resident is not an external liability. Conversely, a domestic-currency bond held by a nonresident is one. The balance of payments records transactions during an interval. The international investment position, or IIP, records external financial assets and liabilities at a date.

The IMF released the seventh edition of its Integrated Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual on 20 March 2025. We cite the March 2025 white-cover, pre-edited BPM7 text actually inspected, not an unspecified final edition. The release recommended country implementation in 2029–2030; publication of a new manual does not establish that a particular dataset has switched methods. Check each release's metadata. See the dated IMF announcement.

BPM7 calls the older BPM6 “primary income” account earned income, “secondary income” transfer income, and “net errors and omissions” statistical discrepancy. These aliases matter when reading older tables. Our signs follow BPM7's financial-account presentation: acquisition of an external asset and incurrence of an external liability are each positive in their own columns; their difference is net lending. The manual's Chapters 2, 8 and 9 and terminology tables specify the framework.

External-account entries from the reporting economy's perspective
Account or columnWhat entersPositive balance means
Current account, CAExports minus imports of goods/services; net earned income; net current transfer incomeCurrent receipts exceed current payments
Capital account, KACapital transfers received less paid, plus disposals less acquisitions of nonproduced nonfinancial assetsNet capital-account receipts
Asset transactions, ATAcquisitions less disposals of external financial assets, including reserve assetsResidents acquire external assets on net
Liability transactions, LTIncurrences less repayments/disposals of external liabilitiesResidents incur external liabilities on net
Financial account, FAAT − LTNet lending to the rest of the world

The capital account is not a synonym for international financial flows. Buying a foreign bond belongs in the financial account; importing a machine belongs in goods trade, with its financing recorded separately. Interest belongs in earned income, whereas repayment of principal reduces a liability. Equity liabilities are not all debt. Direct investment, portfolio investment, derivatives, other investment and reserves distinguish forms of financial exposure; the current-account balance alone does not reveal their composition.

CA + KA = FA = AT − LT in complete, internally consistent records.
SD ≡ FA − (CA + KA), so CA + KA − FA + SD = 0 in the measured presentation.

SD is the statistical discrepancy. It is not a separately observed financing source or automatically evidence of illegal flows. If measured CA + KA is −10 and measured FA is −8, SD is +2; these numbers do not identify which component is wrong. Offsetting measurement errors can also leave SD equal to zero. Some analytical presentations instead define net financial inflow as LT − AT = −FA. Their plus-sign balance equation is compatible with ours only after that definition changes.

Connect the current account to saving without imposing a cause

Let Y be nominal GDP, C private consumption, G government consumption, and I all gross domestic investment, including public investment. Let EI and TI denote net earned and current transfer income from abroad. Using consistent prices and periods,

Y = C + G + I + X − M;
GNDI = Y + EI + TI;
S = GNDI − C − G;
S − I = X − M + EI + TI = CA.

GNDI is gross national disposable income and S is gross national saving. This follows by substitution, not by assuming that investment is financed only domestically. If government purchases include investment, split it out of G and include it in I once. Capital transfers are not current disposable income: net lending is CA + KA, not always CA alone. The identity permits a deficit caused by consumption, investment, income losses or combinations of them; a causal policy claim needs behavioral responses and evidence.

Worked example 1 — Borrowing while net foreign assets improve

Measure every entry in millions of home-currency units H during one synthetic year. Transactions are valued at their event-date prices and exchange rates. All exports and imports below include goods and services. The asset columns show the stated settlement, not an additional sale of output.

A complete synthetic external transaction ledger; million H
EventCAKAPrivate external assetsReserve assetsExternal liabilities
Exports paid into an external deposit100010000
Imports: 117 paid from private deposits, 3 from reserves−1200−117−30
Earned income received80800
Earned income paid−50−500
Current transfers received70700
Current transfers paid−20−200
Capital transfer received02200
New external loan deposited abroad0012012
Total−1225−312

Each row satisfies CA + KA = change in external assets minus change in external liabilities. The importer's domestic payment to obtain the reserve-financed settlement is internal to the economy and is not another external payment. Net exports are −20; EI = 3 and TI = 5 give CA = −12. Total asset transactions are 5 − 3 = 2, so FA = 2 − 12 = −10 = CA + KA. The new loan is not income; both its deposit asset and its liability are recorded.

Opening assets are 150 and liabilities 200, hence net foreign assets are −50. Suppose asset revaluations add 19, liability revaluations add 4, and a resident's emigration removes a foreign financial asset worth 1 from the reporting population, with no other affected positions. The last change is a residence reclassification, not a purchase or current transfer. Closing assets are 150 + 2 + 19 − 1 = 170; liabilities are 200 + 12 + 4 = 216. Net foreign assets finish at −46: the economy borrowed 10 through transactions but gained 15 through net valuation and lost 1 through other volume changes. A current deficit and an improving net position can coexist.

If Y = 200, C = 150, G = 30 and I = 40, the expenditure identity gives net exports −20. GNDI = 208 and S = 28, so S − I = −12. KA = 2 then reduces net borrowing to 10. This reconciliation supplies no welfare ranking of the loan or the investment.

2. Transactions do not explain every balance-sheet change

Write NFA = A − L for the net external financial position in home currency; in our examples this equals net IIP. All holdings are financial claims, with no monetary-gold exception. Superscript T denotes transactions, V valuation and O other volume changes. Subtract the separate asset and liability reconciliations:

NFA₁ = NFA₀ + (AT − LT) + (AV − LV) + (AO − LO)
= NFA₀ + FA + V + O.

Exchange-rate changes and market-price changes can alter positions without financing any new consumption. Residence changes and certain reclassifications also change the reporting boundary. Transactions should use their event-date exchange rates; opening and closing stocks use their respective dates. Translating all flows at the closing exchange rate can falsely move part of a holding gain into transactions. A measured IIP reconciliation can have its own discrepancy; the formula is an accounting requirement, not a guarantee that independently compiled data match.

Fix our quote for the rest of the chapter:

eₜ = H paid for one unit of foreign currency F, with eₜ > 0.
Higher e means depreciation of H; lower e means appreciation of H.

For unchanged foreign-currency assets A* and liabilities L*, with no interest, trades or other price changes during an instantaneous repricing, the valuation contribution is (e₁ − e₀)(A* − L*). For example, 40 F of assets and 70 F of debt at e₀ = 2 imply NFA₀ = −60 H. At e₁ = 5/2, NFA₁ = −75 H. The loss of 15 H is valuation; CA and FA are both zero. Depreciation harms this unhedged net foreign-currency debtor, whereas a net holder of foreign-currency assets gains. Domestic-currency claims, derivatives and different sectors can reverse the aggregate or distributional result.

Interest is not this valuation term. When accrued interest increases the amount owed, it has an earned-income entry and a financial-account counterpart. Identify when it accrues before converting it. A rise in the home value of unchanged principal and the accrual of additional foreign principal are separate changes. BPM7 Chapter 9 explicitly separates transactions, exchange revaluation, other price revaluation and other volume changes.

Gross positions matter even when NFA is zero. An economy with 100 of illiquid foreign assets and 100 of external debt due tomorrow has a different refinancing problem from one with no cross-border positions. Currency, maturity, liquidity, sector, collateral and contingent obligations matter. An improvement in NFA caused by a fall in the market value of the economy's own liabilities can coexist with severe distress; it is not automatically improved ability to pay.

3. The real exchange rate and purchasing power parity

Let P be H per home consumption basket and P* be F per foreign basket. The real exchange rate is

q = eP*/P.

It measures home baskets required to buy one foreign basket. A rise in q is a real depreciation of home: the foreign basket becomes relatively dearer. This is different from the terms of trade, the export-good price divided by the import-good price. It is also different from an index whose publisher uses the reciprocal convention; always inspect its definition.

For one identical tradable good, no transport cost, tariff, tax difference, resale restriction or market power, and unconstrained trade in both directions, a price gap permits buying cheaply and selling dearly. No arbitrage then gives Pj = eP*j, the law of one price. Summing that equality with the same basket quantities gives P = eP*, or absolute PPP, q = 1. Different basket weights, nontradables and distribution costs break that inference. Independently rebased consumer-price indices cannot establish absolute PPP: multiplying one index by an arbitrary constant changes q's level.

The authors' Columbia slides on real exchange rates distinguish good-level arbitrage, basket comparisons and relative price-index movements. Here the examples use explicitly priced baskets; no measured cross-country price level or convergence speed is assumed.

q₁/q₀ = (e₁/e₀)(P*₁/P*₀)/(P₁/P₀).
If q₁ = q₀, then e₁/e₀ = (1 + πH)/(1 + πF),
so exact depreciation d = (πH − πF)/(1 + πF).

This is relative PPP, conditional on a constant real exchange rate. Prices and their gross growth factors must be positive. The familiar d ≈ πH − πF is first order. The log identity is exact: Δln q = Δln e + Δln P* − Δln P. None of these identities guarantees that q remains constant after a productivity, preference or policy shock.

For instance, P rises from 100 to 110 H per basket, P* from 50 to 52 F per basket, and e starts at 2 H/F. Constant q = 1 requires e₁ = 110/52 = 55/26, a depreciation of 3/52 ≈ 5.7692%, rather than exactly six percent. If e instead remains at 2, q₁ = 52/55: home experiences real appreciation. A fixed nominal quote need not imply equal inflation when q changes.

4. Covered interest parity is a financed payoff comparison

At date t, a default-free deposit paying one unit of its own currency at t + 1 costs 1/R in that currency, where R = 1 + i > 0. Negative net interest is permitted while the gross payoff remains positive. Let RH and RF be the two gross returns and Ft,t+1 the forward quote, in H/F, agreed today for exchange at the same maturity. The letter F in this subscripted quote is a price, not the financial-account balance.

Invest 1 H domestically: it becomes RH H. Alternatively buy 1/eₜ F, invest it to obtain RF/eₜ F, and contract today to sell the entire foreign maturity amount forward. The second route delivers Ft,t+1RF/eₜ H with no open currency exposure. If both routes can be borrowed and lent at the stated rates, the higher payoff can be financed by borrowing through the lower-payoff route. With no default, counterparty failure, taxes, spreads, margin costs or quantity restrictions, no arbitrage requires

RH = (Ft,t+1/eₜ)RF,
Ft,t+1 = eₜRH/RF.

This is exact one-period covered interest parity, CIP. Both directions of borrowing matter; a person allowed only to deposit cannot necessarily implement the arbitrage. All cash flows must share maturity and credit quality. The forward rate is a contracted conversion price, not a revealed forecast of the future spot rate.

Worked example 2 — A hedge, an arbitrage and an uncertain return

Set e₀ = 2 H/F, RH = 21/20 and RF = 51/50 for one year. CIP gives F0,1 = 35/17 ≈ 2.058824 H/F. A saver converts 200 H into 100 F, receives 102 F next year and sells all 102 F at the contracted quote to receive 210 H. This equals the domestic deposit payoff. Hedging only the original 100 F would leave two foreign units exposed.

Suppose instead an executable forward quote is 21/10 H/F under the same frictionless funding assumptions. Borrow 200 H at date 0, convert to 100 F and deposit abroad. At date 1 the forward sale of 102 F yields 214.2 H. Repay 210 H and retain 4.2 H. Initial net investment is zero and the terminal payoff is positive in every exchange-rate state. This is the arbitrage that the ideal equality rules out, not a recommendation based on an observed quote.

Remove the hedge. Suppose e₁ is 9/5 or 12/5 with equal probabilities, a supplied conditional distribution. The 100 F investment returns 183.6 or 244.8 H, gross home returns 0.918 and 1.224. Their mean is 1.071, exceeding the domestic gross return 1.05 by 0.021. But the low state loses 26.4 H relative to repaying the 210 H loan. Positive expected profit is not riskless profit. The assumed mean future spot 2.1 differs from the CIP forward 35/17.

Trading costs produce bounds, not an equality at imaginary midpoint rates

Let eb ≤ ea be spot bid and ask: the dealer buys F at the bid and sells F at the ask. Define Fb ≤ Fa similarly for forward exchange. Let RH,l and RH,b be home lending and borrowing gross rates, with lending no higher than borrowing; use analogous foreign rates. Two funded strategies must have nonpositive terminal profit:

(Fb/ea)RF,l ≤ RH,b,
ebRH,l ≤ FaRF,b.

The first borrows 1 H, buys F at the ask, lends abroad and sells proceeds forward at the bid. The second borrows 1 F, sells at the spot bid, lends H and buys the foreign repayment forward at the ask. Equality of borrowing/lending and bid/ask prices collapses these bounds to CIP. They are necessary no-arbitrage checks for these strategies under the stated credit and access assumptions; they are not a full model of every market constraint.

Borio, McCauley, McGuire and Sushko's September 2016 BIS analysis examines hedging demand and costly arbitrage balance sheets. We use its discussion of funding, counterparty, liquidity and balance-sheet constraints to explain why a quoted spread need not be an attainable free profit. We do not import its historical measurements as current data.

5. Uncovered parity adds a risk and expectations assumption

Without a hedge the foreign gross home-currency return is RFeₜ₊₁/eₜ. If the conditional mean exists, define its expected excess over the domestic deposit by

rFX,t ≡ RF Eₜ[eₜ₊₁]/eₜ − RH.

This signed expected excess return is a definition, not automatically an estimated compensation for one particular risk. Uncovered interest parity, UIP, imposes rFX,t = 0. It can follow from risk neutrality in the home-currency payoff, common expectations and unrestricted portfolio adjustment. Risk-neutral real consumption preferences are not enough if the home price level is uncertain. More generally, payoffs in states where funds are especially valuable can command different expected returns. We defer a full stochastic-discount-factor derivation to asset pricing.

The authors' Columbia capital-market slides derive covered payoff comparisons and show why unrestricted capital markets need not imply UIP under risk aversion. Our zero-premium regime case below explicitly imposes the additional expected-return condition.

Under UIP, Eₜ[eₜ₊₁]/eₜ − 1 = RH/RF − 1
= (iH − iF)/(1 + iF).

The approximate interest-differential rule drops the denominator correction. UIP concerns the conditional mean, not each realization. With CIP and UIP together, the forward equals the conditional mean future spot. With CIP alone, it need not. Also E[1/e] generally differs from 1/E[e], and E[ln e] differs from ln E[e]; reversing a quote or taking logs after an expectation changes the object. A regression using realized depreciation combines forecast errors with any risk premium and measurement error. It does not identify all three from one coefficient.

A higher home interest rate can accompany expected depreciation, changing default risk, monetary tightening or news about future prices. Whether today's currency appreciates requires a closure for expected future exchange rates and risk. For example, at fixed Eₜ[eₜ₊₁], RF and rFX,t, the identity eₜ = RFEₜ[eₜ₊₁]/(RH + rFX,t) makes a higher RH lower today's e. That partial comparison is compatible with subsequent expected depreciation; it is not a universal sign prediction.

6. Close a monetary regime before predicting capital flows

Here is a deliberately small current-date model. Commercial banks are absent, so H is directly held central-bank currency/base money; no broad-money multiplier is assumed. Fix real output and the price level during the instantaneous adjustment. Maintained money demand is H/P = a − χiH, with a,χ > 0. Interest is the nominal opportunity cost of noninterest-bearing H. We use only states with H > 0. Because currency is freely storable at zero nominal return here, also impose iH ≥ 0: a desired negative deposit rate lies outside this closure.

The central bank holds domestic securities D measured in H and R units of a foreign reserve asset; reserve quantities earn no interest during this instantaneous operation. Its equity is K, also in H:

D + eR = H + K.

Domestic purchases of securities from residents increase D and H by the purchase amount. A reserve sale at the peg retires H. Reserve revaluation changes K, unless an additional distribution or recapitalization is explicitly introduced. It does not automatically print currency. Domestic securities are treated as fixed-price claims during this short adjustment; bond-price gains, bank credit, fiscal transfers and output responses are outside this model.

Credible fixed quote: the announced ē is maintained through the asset maturity, with no expected change or credit difference and free asset substitution. Then iH = iF. Money demand determines H = P(a − χiF), and the balance sheet determines R = [H + K − D]/ē. The peg requires 0 ≤ iF < a/χ and R ≥ 0 under our no-reserve-borrowing rule. The domestic asset choice is not an independent way to choose H while maintaining all these restrictions.

Floating quote: keep reserve quantity R₀ unchanged and supply a conditional expectation m = E₀[e₁] > 0 and rFX = 0. Given initial e₀ and K₀, mark reserves to market with K = K₀ + (e − e₀)R₀. The balance sheet reduces to H = D + e₀R₀ − K₀. Money demand sets iH, and UIP sets e = mRF/(1 + iH). These equations have one admissible solution when 0 < H ≤ Pa, so the derived rate is nonnegative; outside this range the stated closure fails. The expectation is an external model input, not something proved by the current monetary expansion. This is a conditional asset-and-money-market comparison, not an infinite-horizon equilibrium or welfare theorem.

Worked example 3 — The same domestic purchase under a peg and a float

Take P = 1 H per basket, a = 100 baskets, χ = 100 baskets per unit net interest, iF = 1/20, and initial e₀ = 2 H/F. Initially D = 55 H, R₀ = 20 F, K₀ = 0 and H = 95 H; money demand gives iH = 5%. The central bank buys 2 H of domestic securities from residents, so D becomes 57.

Under the credible peg, money demand still requires H = 95. Selling 1 F of reserves for 2 H reverses the initial currency injection. End stocks are D = 57, R = 19, H = 95, K = 0; 57 + 2(19) = 95. Residents have exchanged 2 H of domestic securities for an external asset worth 2 H, and official external assets have fallen by the same amount. This within-economy portfolio shift does not by itself change aggregate NFA or create a current-account surplus. There is no additional net transaction with the rest of the world in this instantaneous swap.

Under the float, R stays 20 F and H = 57 + 2(20) = 97 H. Money demand implies iH = 3%. With supplied m = 2 H/F, UIP gives e = 2(21/20)/(103/100) = 210/103 ≈ 2.038835 H/F. Equity rises to (210/103 − 2)20 = 80/103 H. The complete balance sheet is 57 + 4,200/103 = 97 + 80/103. The reserve holding gain belongs to equity; treating it as extra H would violate the stated operations. Residents sell domestic securities for the 2 H currency increase; no reserve sale is needed.

Under the original peg, R = (95 − D)/2. At D = 95 reserves are exactly zero; D = 96 would require −1/2 F and fails this regime's constraint. A new external credit line, changed asset choice or changed peg would be a new model. Under the float, D = 60 would give H = 100 and iH = 0; D > 60 violates this currency model's nonnegative-rate domain. These limits are feasibility statements, not predictions of the time an attack occurs. Likewise, a higher supplied m under the float changes the exchange-rate response without changing today's purchase. Expectations and access are part of the result.

The example exposes the restrictions behind the monetary-policy trilemma: under freely substitutable comparable assets and a credible fixed rate, a separate nominal interest-rate path cannot be chosen at will. Capital controls or imperfect substitution can create a wedge; they do not remove every resource or credibility constraint. Sterilizing a reserve sale by purchasing domestic assets tries to preserve H, but with unchanged money demand and parity the original pressure remains in this model. Neither regime is universally preferable: stabilization, balance-sheet currency exposure, credibility, institutional capacity and distribution require a larger analysis.

7. Diagnose an external-balance claim

A deficit may finance productive investment or consumption smoothing; it may also accompany risky currency and maturity mismatches. A surplus may reflect high saving, weak investment, income gains or restrictions. Start with a reconciled ledger, then identify who owes what, when, in which currency and with which contingent promises. Net financial inflow is an accounting counterpart, not a unique explanation of the current account. Large gross inflows and outflows can offset in FA while financing vulnerabilities change.

For an empirical claim that a depreciation improves the current account, specify a horizon, trade volumes and prices, invoicing currencies, elasticities, income payments and the policy shock. Exchange-rate movements may respond to the same news that changes trade and financing. An accounting identity or a parity regression cannot separate those responses on its own. A convincing design explains the exogenous variation, anticipation, competing policies and spillovers, with sensitivity checks and a declared target. Do not treat the synthetic cases as estimated policy multipliers.

Reproducible reconciliation

The offline lab supplies documented synthetic inputs, a standard-library benchmark, preserved exact output and a README. It reconciles each transaction row, the stock bridge, exact parity payoffs, executable bid/ask bounds and the two monetary regimes. Change a rate, settlement entry or reserve limit and explain which identity or maintained condition fails before interpreting the output.

Exercises

  1. Accounts, saving and a discrepancy. In million H, exports are 80, imports 95, earned-income receipts/payments 6/4, current transfers 3/5 and capital transfers 2/1. There are no other capital entries. Asset transactions are −2 and liability transactions +12. Compute CA, KA, FA and SD. With Y = 200, C = 150, G = 30 and I = 35, verify the saving bridge. G is consumption and I already includes 5 of public investment. An independently measured asset transaction total is instead −1. Recompute SD and explain what it identifies.
  2. Stocks, valuation and interest timing. Opening external assets/liabilities are 180/210 H. Their transaction changes are +6/+15, revaluations +8/−4 and other volume changes −2/+1. Compute both closing stocks, FA and the NFA reconciliation. Separately, an external debt has principal 100 F at e₀ = 2. The quote jumps to 3 before any interest accrues. Interest of 5 F then accrues at that end-date quote and is added to the debt; there is no payment or other flow. Split the change in its home-currency liability into principal valuation and transactions. State the CA and FA entries.
  3. Exact PPP and quotation. A comparable basket costs 120 H at home and 60 F abroad at date 0, with e₀ = 2. At date 1 the prices are 132 H and 63 F, while actual e₁ = 11/5. Find q at both dates, the nominal and real depreciation rates, the exchange rate required by relative PPP and the exact PPP depreciation rate. How much does the reciprocal F/H value of H fall? Explain why two arbitrary CPI levels cannot replace these priced baskets in a test of absolute PPP.
  4. Both directions of covered arbitrage. Set e = 3/2 H/F, RH = 27/25 and RF = 51/50, with the frictionless assumptions of Section 4. Derive the parity forward. At forward 81/50, construct a funded trade starting with a loan of 150 H. At forward 39/25, construct the reverse trade starting with a loan of 100 F. Show all maturity cash flows and profits in H. What fails if borrowing and lending rates differ?
  5. Expected returns are not guaranteed returns. Use Worked example 2's distribution, e₀ and deposit rates. Calculate expected depreciation, the depreciation implied by UIP, rFX, and E[1/e₁] versus 1/E[e₁]. Explain why the observed home/foreign rate pair plus CIP does not determine the actual conditional mean exchange rate or a profitable riskless carry trade. State two possible reasons a realized-depreciation regression need not identify risk compensation.
  6. Use executable quotes. Spot bid/ask are 1.99/2.01 H/F and forward bid/ask 2.02/2.06. Home lending/borrowing gross rates are 1.04/1.06 and foreign lending/borrowing gross rates 1.01/1.03. Compute the terminal profit per 1 H borrowed through the first strategy in Section 4, and per 1 F borrowed through the second, expressing both profits in H. Do either violate the stated bounds? Explain why testing equality with midpoint quotes and midpoint interest rates would not establish an executable arbitrage.
  7. A foreign rate shock and reserve feasibility. Return to Worked example 3's initial balance sheet, with D = 55 and no domestic purchase. Raise iF to 8%. Under the credible peg compute iH, H and R, showing the central bank and resident portfolio changes. Under the float keep R = 20 and supplied m = 2: compute iH, e and K. In a separate original-rate peg case set D = 95 and then 96. Identify feasibility and explain why a constant money supply, a fixed exchange rate and an independent rate target cannot all be imposed here.
  8. Critique and transfer. A memo says: “The current account improved, so the country became safer; depreciation caused the improvement; its high domestic rate guarantees a currency gain; the central bank can sterilize indefinitely.” Give a structured response using stocks versus flows, gross/currency/maturity positions, causal identification, covered versus uncovered returns and the regime constraint. Design one empirical comparison for the depreciation claim, naming its estimand, timing, required variation, a threat and a diagnostic. State what evidence could change your judgment.
Complete solutions

  1. Net exports are −15, EI = 2 and TI = −2, so CA = −15. KA = 1. FA = −2 − 12 = −14, hence SD = −14 − (−15 + 1) = 0. GDP spending is 150 + 30 + 35 − 15 = 200; GNDI = 200 + 2 − 2 = 200 and S = 20. Thus S − I = −15 = CA, while net lending is −14. The 5 of public investment is already in I; deducting it from saving as consumption would count it twice. With measured asset transactions −1, measured FA = −13 and SD = +1. The residual flags an inconsistency but does not reveal whether receipts, payments, assets, liabilities or timing are mismeasured. A zero discrepancy in the first table also cannot prove every input correct.

  2. Assets close at 180 + 6 + 8 − 2 = 192; liabilities at 210 + 15 − 4 + 1 = 222. Opening and closing NFA are both −30. FA = 6 − 15 = −9; V = 8 − (−4) = 12 and O = −2 − 1 = −3. Hence −30 − 9 + 12 − 3 = −30. With KA = 0 and consistent accounts the implied CA would be −9, not zero.

    In the separate debt case, unchanged principal revalues from 200 to 300 H, a liability valuation increase of 100. End-date interest is 5 × 3 = 15 H and increases the liability through a transaction. Closing debt is 105 × 3 = 315 H. Its total increase 115 is 100 valuation plus 15 transaction. Earned-income debit gives CA = −15; liability incurrence +15 gives FA = −15. No interest is paid in cash, but accrual still enters income and its financing. Calling all 115 valuation, or adding interest again after valuing 105 F, would be wrong.

  3. q₀ = 2(60)/120 = 1 and q₁ = (11/5)(63)/132 = 21/20. Nominal depreciation is (11/5)/2 − 1 = 1/10; real depreciation is 1/20. Relative PPP requires e₁ = 2(132/120)/(63/60) = 44/21, giving depreciation 1/21 ≈ 4.7619%. The first-order inflation difference is 10% − 5% = 5%, which is not the exact answer. The reciprocal quote falls from 1/2 to 5/11 F/H; its proportional change is (5/11)/(1/2) − 1 = −1/11 ≈ −9.0909%. Reversing a quote does not simply negate a finite percentage change. Separately normalized CPI levels have arbitrary scale; their changes can support a relative real-rate calculation, but their level ratio does not price a common basket.

  4. The parity forward is (3/2)(27/25)/(51/50) = 27/17 ≈ 1.588235 H/F. At 81/50, borrow 150 H, buy and deposit 100 F, then receive 102 F. Sell them forward for 102(81/50) = 4,131/25 = 165.24 H and repay 150(27/25) = 162 H. Profit is 81/25 = 3.24 H.

    At 39/25, borrow 100 F, sell for 150 H and invest to receive 162 H. Buy the foreign repayment of 102 F forward for 102(39/25) = 3,978/25 = 159.12 H. Repay the foreign loan and retain 72/25 = 2.88 H. Both strategies start with zero net wealth and cover all foreign obligations. Different funding and deposit rates require using the actual borrowing and lending legs; the single-rate equality may be replaced by bounds and neither calculated profit need remain attainable.

  5. The mean future spot is 21/10, so expected depreciation is 1/20 = 5%. UIP instead requires (21/20)/(51/50) − 1 = 1/34 ≈ 2.9412%. Expected foreign gross home return is (51/50)(21/10)/2 = 1071/1000; thus rFX = 21/1000, or 2.1 percentage points. The mean reciprocal is (1/2)(5/9 + 5/12) = 35/72, whereas the reciprocal mean is 10/21. Their difference is 5/504 > 0. CIP determines the forward from executable covered returns, not the unhedged mean. The low state loses relative to the home deposit, so expected gain cannot establish arbitrage. A realized-return regression mixes exchange-rate forecast errors, changing risk premia, endogenous policy/news and measurement or omitted-variable problems. Any two concrete explanations, tied to the regression's timing, satisfy that part.

  6. For 1 H borrowed, the foreign deposit and forward sale deliver (2.02/2.01)(1.01) = 10,201/10,050 H. Repayment is 1.06, leaving −226/5,025 H ≈ −0.044975. For 1 F borrowed, the home investment pays 1.99(1.04) = 2.0696 H and the forward foreign repayment costs 2.06(1.03) = 2.1218 H. Profit is −261/5,000 H = −0.0522. Neither is profitable under the stated access assumptions. Midpoints are not prices at which all required purchases, sales, borrowings and loans can be executed; an apparent midpoint differential need not defeat either inequality.

  7. Under the peg, iH = 0.08 and H = 100 − 100(0.08) = 92 H. Reserves are (92 − 55)/2 = 37/2 F. The central bank sells 3/2 F and retires 3 H; residents exchange 3 H of currency for the external asset. The balance sheet reads 55 + 2(37/2) = 92, with K = 0.

    Under the float, unchanged D and R imply H = 95 and iH = 0.05. The supplied expectation gives e = 2(1.08)/(1.05) = 72/35 H/F. Equity is (72/35 − 2)20 = 8/7 H. Then 55 + (72/35)20 = 95 + 8/7. The reserve quantity is unchanged; the higher home value is a holding gain. Under the separate original-rate peg, D = 95 gives R = 0 and is feasible at the boundary; D = 96 requires R = −1/2 and is infeasible without a changed rule or financing source. Parity fixes the comparable interest rate under the credible peg; money demand fixes H, and the balance sheet then fixes R. Adding an inconsistent independent target overdetermines the system.

  8. A strong response asks whether the improvement is a transaction balance, a valuation gain or a recession-driven reduction in imports, and reconciles it with KA, FA and the IIP. Safety also depends on gross amounts, maturities, currencies, creditors, liquid reserves and contingent obligations; NFA alone is insufficient. Currency changes can be endogenous to the same news that changes trade. Higher nominal interest does not guarantee an exchange gain, and a forward hedge has a contracted price and financing costs. Sterilization under this chapter's free-substitution peg leaves the pressure in place and cannot violate the nonnegative-reserve constraint.

    One illustrative design targets the effect over four quarters of an unexpected exchange-rate policy change on the current account and its components. It needs a comparison group or exposure-based contrast plausibly unaffected by the shock, a measured announcement surprise, consistent pre-policy outcomes and controls justified by the estimand. The identifying claim is that absent the shock the treated and comparison outcomes would have evolved comparably, conditional on the specified design. Anticipation, simultaneous fiscal/trade changes, common demand news, selection into currency exposure and spillovers threaten it. Pre-announcement patterns, placebo dates, alternative exposure measures and sensitivity to concurrent events can diagnose some failures; passing them does not prove the identifying assumption. Report uncertainty and separate trade quantities, prices and earned-income effects. Evidence about credible identification, maturity refinancing, hedges, reserve access and intervention costs could change the assessment. Grade for a coherent estimand and design, explicit assumptions, at least one concrete diagnostic, and the five requested economic distinctions; agreement with a preferred policy is not required.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back: use one transaction and one currency revaluation to explain why CA is not the change in NFA. Draw the two covered investment routes with currencies at every arrow. Then explain why the same domestic securities purchase has different reserve and exchange-rate consequences under the two stated regimes.

Teach-back checklist

A complete explanation names the reporting residents, FA sign, capital-account contribution and separate valuation/other-volume terms. It keeps interest accrual distinct from principal revaluation, hedges the entire maturity amount, states the funding and default assumptions behind CIP, and distinguishes UIP's conditional mean from a guarantee. For regimes, it uses both money demand and the central-bank balance sheet, accounts for valuation in equity, states reserve feasibility and identifies the supplied expectation.

Delayed check: without notes, take CA = −7, KA = 1 and FA = −5. Find SD. Opening NFA is −20, valuation +4 and other changes −1; using the measured FA, find the reconciled closing NFA. With e = 3/2, RH = 26/25 and RF = 1, find the CIP forward. Does that determine the mean future spot? In the original-rate peg, what is R when D = 91?

Delayed-check answer

SD = −5 − (−7 + 1) = +1. The stock bridge gives −20 − 5 + 4 − 1 = −22, conditional on those measured inputs and no additional IIP discrepancy. The forward is (3/2)(26/25) = 39/25 H/F. Identifying it with the expected future spot additionally requires UIP; neither equality guarantees the realized quote. Peg reserves are (95 − 91)/2 = 2 F.

Further study and connection

These derivations do not establish a universal current-account target, exchange-rate forecast or preferred regime. Richer models add endogenous output and prices, asset risk, heterogeneous balance sheets, reserve borrowing and intertemporal fiscal backing. The next chapter, Crises, policy regimes and macroeconomic judgment, combines external funding with bank liquidity, solvency and policy constraints. The accounts and dates here provide the checks those scenarios must pass.

Sources and further study

  • IMF Press Release 25/072 — IMF and the Statistical Community Release New Global Standards for Macroeconomic Statistics (20 March 2025) — Dated release of BPM7 and distinction between publication and recommended country implementation; exact white-cover version scope.
  • International Monetary Fund — Integrated Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual, Seventh Edition: March 2025 White Cover (Pre-Edited) Version — Resident external accounts, financial-account signs, statistical discrepancy, saving-current-account bridge, integrated IIP, valuation and residence reclassification; BPM7 terminology mapped to older BPM6 labels.
  • Stephanie Schmitt-Grohé, Martín Uribe and Michael Woodford — International Macroeconomics: A Modern Approach, Chapter 9 author slides: The Real Exchange Rate and Purchasing Power Parity (2022) — Method route for law of one price, real exchange-rate direction, absolute versus relative PPP and basket/price-index distinctions.
  • Stephanie Schmitt-Grohé, Martín Uribe and Michael Woodford — International Macroeconomics: A Modern Approach, Chapter 11 author slides: International Capital Market Integration (6 September 2022) — Covered investment and arbitrage paths, conditional expected uncovered returns and why free capital mobility alone does not imply UIP.
  • Claudio Borio, Robert McCauley, Patrick McGuire and Vladyslav Sushko — Covered interest parity lost: understanding the cross-currency basis (BIS Quarterly Review, September 2016) — Primary author discussion of executable covered positions, FX hedging, bid/ask and funding frictions, counterparty/liquidity risks and costly balance sheets.
